paragraphs: Data augmentation expands a training set by transforming examples while preserving their labels. This paper develops a theoretical account of how those transformations influence learning. Its first approach models augmentation as a Markov process, describing transformations through probabilistic transitions. Within this formulation, kernels arise naturally even when the eventual classifier is not a kernel method.

The second approach examines kernel classifiers directly. It shows that augmentation can be approximated through two components: averaging features at first order and regularizing their variation at second order. This separates the effect of combining transformed representations from the effect of discouraging sensitivity to transformations. The analysis also connects augmentation to invariant kernels, tangent propagation, and robust optimization.

Proof-of-concept applications illustrate possible practical uses of the theory. These include reducing computation when training with augmented data and predicting whether a transformation will help before training begins. The findings position augmentation as a process whose effects can be analyzed and sometimes anticipated, while the practical demonstrations remain proof-of-concept results.
icml-2019-a-kernel-theory-of-modern-data.tldr: A theoretical framework explains data augmentation through kernels, feature averaging, and variance regularization, with proof-of-concept uses for more efficient training.

paragraphs: This paper studies survival prediction across several cancer types. Instead of fitting a separate survival model to every dataset, the authors develop Path2MSurv, a multitask method that learns across related cancer datasets. The motivation is that related prediction problems can benefit from being analyzed together, allowing the learning process to use information shared across tasks.

Path2MSurv uses multiple kernel learning and incorporates cancer-related pathways and gene sets into survival analysis. Its design therefore combines two kinds of structure: relationships among cancer datasets and biological groupings of genes. The method can also identify pathways or gene sets that are useful for predicting survival in different cancer types, connecting its predictions to these biological groupings.

The evaluation uses Cancer Genome Atlas gene expression profiles from 7,655 patients across 20 cancer types. Path2MSurv delivers better or comparable predictive performance against random survival forests, survival support vector machines, and its single-task variant. These findings support the usefulness of the combined approach without implying that it outperforms every comparator on every cancer type.
icml-2019-a-multitask-multiple-kernel-le.tldr: Path2MSurv combines learning across cancer types with pathway information to achieve better or comparable survival prediction against the tested alternatives.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to make effective use of a limited labeling budget. This paper improves IWAL, an online importance-weighted active learning algorithm, by using information about disagreements among candidate hypotheses. The central idea is that the structure of those disagreements can guide how the learner updates the collection of hypotheses it considers.

The first enhancement, IWAL-D, uses a disagreement graph to prune that collection more aggressively. The authors show improvements in both generalization performance and label complexity relative to IWAL, expressing the improvement through a disagreement graph coefficient. This ties the benefit to a property of the hypothesis disagreements rather than presenting it only as an experimental observation.

The second enhancement, IZOOM, adaptively focuses on the current version space and reduces the best error achievable within its changing hypothesis class. The paper provides theoretical guarantees that accommodate this changing set. Experiments on multiple datasets also show better test performance than IWAL at the same labeling budget, supporting the practical value of both enhancements.
icml-2019-active-learning-with-disagreem.tldr: IWAL-D and IZOOM use hypothesis disagreements to improve active learning guarantees and test performance at a fixed labeling budget.

paragraphs: A controlled experiment can support causal conclusions about its study population without automatically supporting the same conclusions elsewhere. This paper separates two obstacles to generalization: differences between populations or causal mechanisms, and preferential selection of people into the study. Both can make experimental findings misleading when applied to a new population.

The authors investigate when adjustment using measured covariates can correct these problems together. They derive complete graphical conditions for deciding whether a proposed set of covariates is admissible for adjustment in this setting. The contribution is a way to determine which adjustment choices are justified by the represented causal assumptions, rather than assuming that adding more variables will solve the problem.

They also develop an algorithm that enumerates all admissible adjustment sets with a polynomial-time delay between outputs. This guarantee concerns the delay between sets, not the total number of possible sets. Having multiple valid choices is useful when variables differ in measurement cost or accessibility, allowing practical considerations to inform the final adjustment strategy.
icml-2019-adjustment-criteria-for-genera.tldr: Complete graphical criteria identify when covariate adjustment can generalize experimental effects despite population differences and sampling bias.

paragraphs: A standard route from online learning to stochastic convex optimization guarantees the quality of an average of successive iterates. The individual iterates do not automatically receive comparable guarantees. This paper introduces a black-box modification of online learning algorithms so that the resulting iterates themselves converge to the optimum in stochastic settings.

For smooth losses, the authors combine this modification with optimistic online learning. They obtain a convergence rate of O(L/T^(3/2) + σ/√T), where T counts iterations, L describes smoothness, and σ² is the gradient variance. The two terms distinguish the contribution associated with smoothness from the contribution associated with noisy gradients.

A further reduction converts adaptive online algorithms into methods with the optimal accelerated rate Õ(L/T² + σ/√T), while retaining Õ(1/√T) convergence for nonsmooth problems. The tilde notation suppresses logarithmic factors. These methods automatically adapt to L and σ without requiring either in advance, making the stated guarantees compatible with uncertainty about the problem's smoothness and noise.
icml-2019-anytime-online-to-batch-optimi.tldr: Black-box reductions give individual optimization iterates convergence guarantees and adaptive accelerated rates without prior knowledge of smoothness or gradient noise.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can reduce the number of hyperparameter settings that need evaluation, but each evaluation may still require a lengthy training run. This paper asks how intermediate training information, such as validation accuracy after an epoch, can help avoid spending additional epochs on settings that will ultimately perform poorly.

The proposed method, BO-BOS, combines Gaussian process upper confidence bound optimization with Bayesian optimal stopping. The optimization component chooses promising settings efficiently in terms of function evaluations. The stopping component addresses the cost within each evaluation by deciding when to end training early. Together, they address both which experiments to run and how long to continue them.

With the authors' specified stopping parameters, BO-BOS preserves the asymptotic no-regret property of GP-UCB. That preservation is conditional on the stated parameter choice, which has an exploration–exploitation interpretation. Empirical evaluations cover hyperparameter optimization and two other applications, illustrating the approach's generality and its use in improving efficiency measured in training epochs.
icml-2019-bayesian-optimization-meets-ba.tldr: BO-BOS combines Bayesian optimization with principled early stopping to save training epochs while preserving asymptotic no-regret behavior under specified parameters.

paragraphs: Density estimation aims to learn a probability distribution from data. Iterative methods repeatedly refine that estimate, but the paper identifies a gap between the availability of such methods and convincing convergence guarantees. Earlier guarantees, as characterized by the authors, depend on assumptions that can be demanding or difficult to verify.

The proposed approach combines variational divergence minimization, associated with f-GAN, and classical supervised boosting theory. Its key construction uses classifiers as sufficient statistics of an exponential family. This gives the classifiers a direct role in specifying the density model, providing a mathematical connection between combining supervised predictors and improving a distribution estimate.

The authors prove geometric convergence under assumptions they describe as very weak, presenting this as the first density estimation algorithm with that combination of guarantees. Geometric convergence means the relevant error bound decreases by a multiplicative factor across iterations. The analysis also improves the variational characterization of f-GAN, so the contribution includes both an estimation algorithm and a refinement of its theoretical foundation.
icml-2019-boosted-density-estimation-rem.tldr: Combining boosting with variational divergence minimization yields a density estimator with provable geometric convergence under very weak assumptions.

paragraphs: Fair representation learning becomes more demanding when fairness must account for several sensitive attributes and their combinations. This paper addresses that problem by learning a compact representation that remains useful for reconstruction and prediction while supporting different fairness requirements. Its design draws inspiration from disentangled representation learning.

The proposed flexibility lies in modifying the representation at test time to achieve subgroup demographic parity for multiple sensitive attributes and their conjunctions. This means the intended fairness target can concern groups defined by combinations of attributes, as well as groups defined by individual attributes. The method is designed to adapt a learned representation to these different targets.

Empirical results show that a single representation can support fair classification tasks with new target labels and subgroup definitions. The resulting encoder does not require sensitive attributes during inference. These findings support the practical adaptability of the approach; the fairness criterion being addressed is subgroup demographic parity, so the result should be understood in terms of that specific goal.
icml-2019-flexibly-fair-representation-l.tldr: A disentanglement-inspired representation can be adapted at test time for subgroup demographic parity across multiple sensitive attributes and new classification tasks.

paragraphs: Many linear transforms can be expressed as dense matrix multiplication yet have specialized algorithms that are much faster. This paper asks how much of that algorithmic structure can be learned automatically. The authors introduce a parameterization of divide-and-conquer methods based on products of sparse matrices, capable of representing a broad class of transforms.

This structure supplies a prior about what an efficient algorithm should look like while allowing its parameters to be learned. For example, the method recovers the O(N log N) Cooley–Tukey fast Fourier transform to machine precision for dimensions up to 1,024. This demonstrates recovery of an efficient computational procedure within the tested size range.

The same formulation can replace generic matrices inside learning systems with efficient, compressible transformations. In a task compressing a single-hidden-layer network on CIFAR-10, it exceeds unconstrained matrices by 3.9 classification accuracy points while using 40 times fewer parameters and achieving fourfold faster inference. These reported gains concern that evaluated task, alongside the broader demonstration of transform learning.
icml-2019-learning-fast-algorithms-for-l.tldr: Learned butterfly factorizations recover fast linear-transform algorithms and provide compact transformations with strong results on a network-compression task.

paragraphs: Group convolutions extend ordinary convolution by transforming filters through operations such as rotations and flips as well as translations. These transformations provide useful structure for learning, but defining exact rotations of a small filter on a square pixel grid is difficult. This paper focuses on learning filter transformations for rotations and translations.

The method learns a filter basis together with rotated versions of that basis. Each filter is represented by coefficients that stay unchanged under rotation. Rotating the filter then means switching to the corresponding basis while retaining those coefficients. This creates a learned form of weight sharing across orientations and places the transformation structure inside the filter representation.

The authors demonstrate feature maps with low sensitivity to input rotations and high performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Low sensitivity is the stated result, rather than exact invariance to every possible rotation. The approach matters because it provides a practical way to learn how filters transform when a precise hand-designed rotation rule is awkward on the underlying pixel grid.
icml-2019-learning-to-convolve-a-general.tldr: Learning rotated filter bases enables generalized weight sharing and produces rotation-insensitive features with high performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: This paper studies how experience with earlier tasks can improve learning on new tasks drawn from an unknown distribution. The underlying learner uses stochastic gradient descent with a regularizer based on squared Euclidean distance from a bias vector. That vector provides a shared reference point toward which task-specific solutions are encouraged.

The authors derive an average excess-risk bound that quantifies the potential benefit of this bias compared with the unbiased case. They then introduce a meta-algorithm that estimates the bias online as tasks arrive. The method has a small memory footprint and low computational cost, and its analysis provides guarantees about generalization to new tasks.

A central conclusion is conditional: the approach has a significant advantage over learning tasks independently with ordinary SGD when the number of observed tasks grows and variation among tasks is relatively small. This identifies task relatedness as part of the setting supporting the benefit. Numerical experiments also demonstrate the method's effectiveness, complementing the theoretical account of when shared experience can help.
icml-2019-learning-to-learn-stochastic-g.tldr: An online meta-algorithm learns a shared regularization bias that can improve SGD on new tasks when enough sufficiently related tasks are available.

paragraphs: Preconditioning changes how an optimization method scales its updates across parameter directions. This paper introduces an online convex optimization algorithm whose regret guarantee lies between guarantees associated with an optimal preconditioning matrix and a diagonal preconditioning matrix. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison choice, so the result concerns performance across the online sequence.

The stated bound is never worse than the bound obtained through diagonal preconditioning. In certain settings, it even surpasses bounds for algorithms using full-matrix preconditioning. The qualification matters: the paper does not claim universal superiority over full-matrix methods. Its computational result is that the algorithm has the same time and space complexity as online gradient descent.

Together, these properties offer stronger adaptive guarantees without increasing the computational complexity class relative to that simple reference method. The analysis also introduces techniques that streamline earlier regret arguments and improve logarithmic factors. The paper concludes with benchmarks on synthetic data and deep learning tasks, placing its theoretical and computational contributions alongside empirical evaluation.
icml-2019-matrix-free-preconditioning-in.tldr: A matrix-free online optimizer offers regret bounds at least as good as diagonal preconditioning with the time and space complexity of gradient descent.

paragraphs: Minimal Achievable Sufficient Statistic Learning defines a training objective around retaining sufficient information with minimal representation. Its minima are minimal sufficient statistics relative to the class of functions being optimized, such as deep networks. This qualification is central: the notion of minimality is tied to what that function class can achieve.

To derive the objective, the authors introduce Conserved Differential Information, or CDI. This information-theoretic quantity is designed to remain useful when continuous random variables depend deterministically on one another, as a network's output depends on its input. The paper contrasts this usefulness with standard mutual information in that setting, making CDI a foundation for the proposed learning objective.

Experiments assess networks trained with MASS Learning on supervised learning, regularization, and uncertainty quantification benchmarks. The reported performance is competitive across these areas. The contribution therefore combines a representation-learning objective with a quantity that supports its derivation and empirical evidence of practical usefulness. The theoretical characterization concerns the objective's minima; the experimental claim concerns the performance of trained networks.
icml-2019-minimal-achievable-sufficient-.tldr: MASS Learning targets minimal sufficient representations within a function class using a new information measure suited to deterministic continuous networks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to formalize an adversary with limited resources that can seriously obstruct learning. It examines the interaction among adversarial capabilities, classifier choices, and losses satisfying the statistical requirement of being proper. The authors identify a sufficient property of an adversary class for it to be harmful to learning.

That property involves a measure of harmfulness generalizing integral probability metrics. The result applies to all proper losses. For a popular subset, optimizing the measure appears to be independent of the loss, a qualified observation rather than an unconditional conclusion. When classifiers are Lipschitz, the optimization takes an optimal-transport form that compresses class-conditional distributions within a limited budget.

Toy experiments also show that training against an adversary of this kind can improve generalization when its budget is sufficiently large. This empirical observation sits alongside the theoretical account of adversarial harmfulness: an adversary capable of making learning difficult can also be useful during training. The improvement is reported for the toy experiments and the specified budget condition.
icml-2019-monge-blunts-bayes-hardness-re.tldr: A sufficient condition characterizes harmful resource-limited adversaries, connecting Lipschitz classifiers to optimal transport and revealing generalization benefits in toy experiments.

paragraphs: Online learning with sleeping experts allows some candidate predictors to be unavailable on a given round. Feedback graphs add another complication: the learner's choice determines which experts' losses it can observe. This paper studies the combination, initially assuming that loss observations and the set of unavailable experts are independent.

Under that assumption, the authors extend a classical sleeping-experts algorithm and prove matching upper and lower bounds on sleeping regret. Their main contribution then relaxes independence. They introduce a more general regret notion and an algorithm with theoretical guarantees, broadening the framework to accommodate dependencies excluded by the initial analysis.

The authors apply the framework to online prediction with abstention, where the learner may decline to predict while paying a specified cost. This creates a concrete setting in which prediction choices and available feedback must be handled together. Experiments on several real-world datasets show substantial improvements over multiple online abstention algorithms, providing empirical support for this application of the more general framework.
icml-2019-online-learning-with-sleeping-.tldr: A generalized sleeping-experts framework relaxes independence assumptions about feedback and availability, with theoretical guarantees and improved online abstention results.

paragraphs: Source code continually introduces new words through variable names, method names, and other identifiers. This changing vocabulary creates difficulties for code models built using natural language processing techniques that are not designed for such openness. The paper introduces a graph-structured cache to represent newly encountered words explicitly.

The cache creates a node for each new word and connects that node to the word's occurrences in the code. This preserves a relationship between an identifier and the places where it is used. The authors combine this structure with graph neural network models for supervised learning on code, making the cache part of a model that can reason over graph relationships.

The combined approach improves performance on both code completion and variable naming. For variable naming, the reported improvement exceeds 100% in relative terms. These improvements come with a moderate increase in computation time. The results show that explicitly linking new vocabulary to its code occurrences can provide useful information for the evaluated prediction tasks.
icml-2019-open-vocabulary-learning-on-so.tldr: A graph-structured cache links new code words to their occurrences, improving code completion and variable naming with moderately higher computation.

paragraphs: Exploration can cause a reinforcement learning agent's performance to vary substantially during training. This paper proposes policy certificates that describe the quality of the next policy before it is executed. The certificates bound its return and its gap from optimal performance, giving people information they can use to decide whether to intervene.

The authors introduce two algorithms that produce certificates and a theoretical framework for analyzing both policy quality and certificate quality. This makes accountability an explicit algorithmic output. A certificate provides bounds on the next episode's policy, supporting an assessment of whether the certified quality is satisfactory before proceeding.

For tabular Markov decision processes, certificate computation can also improve the sample efficiency of optimism-based exploration. One algorithm achieves minimax-optimal probably approximately correct bounds up to lower-order terms. It also matches existing minimax regret bounds and slightly improves them in some settings. These results show that producing information for oversight can coexist with strong learning-efficiency guarantees in the analyzed setting.
icml-2019-policy-certificates-towards-ac.tldr: Policy certificates bound upcoming policy quality for human oversight and can also improve exploration efficiency in tabular reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Structured outliers can make high-dimensional learning methods unreliable even when only a small fraction of the data is corrupted. Sever is a meta-algorithm designed to strengthen an existing learner, such as least squares or stochastic gradient descent, against these outliers. The approach allows robustness to be added around a base learning procedure.

The method combines theoretical guarantees with a scalable computational requirement. Beyond running the underlying learner, it requires computing the top singular vector of a particular n-by-d matrix. This identifies the additional linear-algebra operation involved, making computational cost part of the proposed method's appeal.

Experiments on spam classification and drug design report substantially greater robustness than several baselines. With 1% corruption on spam data, Sever obtains 7.4% test error versus 13.4–20.5% for baselines, with 3% on uncorrupted data. With 10% corruption on drug data, its mean-squared error is 1.42 versus 1.51–2.33, with 1.23 on uncorrupted data. These results show reduced damage from corruption, while performance remains below the uncorrupted reference.
icml-2019-sever-a-robust-meta-algorithm-.tldr: Sever strengthens existing learners against structured outliers, with theoretical guarantees and substantial robustness gains on two evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Set functions predict from collections whose size can vary and whose ordering should not affect the result. This paper proposes using shape constraints to express domain knowledge about how such predictions should behave. These constraints are intended to regularize the model and make its responses easier to understand.

The authors adapt monotonic constraints to set functions and introduce two additional constraints that generalize the conditioning role of weights in a weighted mean. They show how deep lattice networks can train ordinary functions and set functions satisfying these requirements. They also propose a semantic feature engine, a nonlinear estimator that applies constrained set functions to compound sparse categorical features.

Experiments on real-world data achieve accuracy similar to deep sets or deep neural networks while providing guarantees about model behavior. The benefit is therefore the combination of competitive predictive performance and specified behavioral constraints. Those guarantees can make explanation and debugging easier because users have explicit expectations about how the model is allowed to respond.
icml-2019-shape-constraints-for-set-func.tldr: Shape-constrained set functions encode domain knowledge and provide behavioral guarantees while achieving accuracy similar to the tested neural alternatives.

paragraphs: Some inputs are better represented as probability measures or point clouds than as a single fixed-length vector. Such inputs contain unordered observations, potentially with different weights and varying numbers of points. This paper develops a deep learning framework that explicitly accommodates those properties rather than requiring an ordered sequence or fixed-size vector representation.

Its building blocks include push-forward operators, which map measures to measures, and integration steps, which connect measures with ordinary Euclidean representations. These operations allow networks to transform an input distribution while also connecting distribution-valued data to familiar vector-valued computations. The design addresses permutation invariance as well as changes in weights and cardinality.

The framework supports discriminative models for classification or dimensionality reduction, generative models that synthesize measures, and recurrent pipelines for predicting measure dynamics. The paper analyzes the building blocks theoretically, discusses approximation capabilities and robustness to perturbations, and evaluates architectures on discriminative and generative tasks. Its central contribution is a shared architectural foundation for several kinds of learning with distribution-valued inputs.
icml-2019-stochastic-deep-networks-72168.tldr: A deep learning framework processes probability measures and variable-size point clouds through measure transformations and integration.

paragraphs: The paper studies a selection problem in which both cost and benefit are submodular set functions. The objective is to obtain benefit above a specified threshold while minimizing cost. Because these quantities depend on the selected collection, evaluating a candidate solution requires access to the benefit function.

Existing approximation guarantees for the greedy algorithm assume an exact value oracle: a way to obtain the benefit of a set precisely. The authors focus on applications where that assumption is unrealistic because benefit is difficult to compute. They derive two approximation ratios for the setting where only approximate benefit evaluations are available, bringing evaluation uncertainty into the performance analysis.

The two ratios are incomparable, meaning neither provides the stronger guarantee in every case. A case study on the Influence Threshold problem in online social networks shows that the ratios can take empirically relevant values. The contribution therefore extends the theoretical treatment of the problem to imperfect benefit estimates and demonstrates the relevance of those bounds in a concrete application.
icml-2019-submodular-cost-submodular-cov.tldr: Two incomparable approximation guarantees address submodular covering when benefit values are available only approximately.

paragraphs: TarMAC addresses communication among reinforcement learning agents cooperating in environments where each agent has only partial information. Its architecture learns both message content and intended recipients. The targeting behavior is learned from the reward for completing the task, without separate supervision specifying how the agents should communicate.

The architecture also supports several communication rounds before agents act. This gives the group repeated opportunities to coordinate within a decision step. Learning recipients and allowing multiple exchanges address different parts of the communication problem: directing information toward particular agents and enabling coordination to develop over more than one round.

Evaluations span tasks with different difficulties and agent counts, including two-dimensional shape layouts, simulated traffic junctions, and three-dimensional indoor environments. The authors report benefits from targeted and multi-round communication and describe the learned strategies as interpretable and intuitive. Extensions to mixed and competitive environments also improve performance and sample complexity over recent state-of-the-art approaches in the reported evaluations, suggesting usefulness beyond purely cooperative tasks.
icml-2019-tarmac-targeted-multi-agent-co.tldr: TarMAC learns what agents should communicate and to whom, using task rewards and multiple communication rounds to improve coordination.

paragraphs: A common model of teaching seeks the smallest labeled example set that uniquely identifies a target concept. Such a teacher usually needs to know the learner's hypothesis class. This paper studies the harder case in which the learner's internal representation and hypothesis class are unknown, making the learner a black box.

The authors establish a sharp distinction between teaching with and without interaction. Within their setting, a teacher that cannot interact with the learner can do no better than supplying random examples. With interaction, however, the teacher can efficiently find a teaching set that is provably a good approximation to the optimal set. Interaction therefore supplies information needed to make example selection effective.

The paper illustrates the approach through training-set reduction for families of classifiers. The goal is to find an approximately smallest subset of training instances that produces the same classifier as the full dataset. This connects the teaching result to a concrete data-reduction task while preserving the distinction between an approximate minimum and an exactly smallest set.
icml-2019-teaching-a-black-box-learner-5.tldr: Interaction enables efficient, approximately optimal teaching of a black-box learner and supports reducing training sets while preserving the learned classifier.

paragraphs: A policy in reinforcement learning determines a value function describing expected returns from states. This paper studies the geometry of all value functions obtainable in a Markov decision process with finite state and action spaces. Its main result characterizes this space as a general polytope, giving the collection a concrete geometric structure.

The analysis develops structural relationships between policies and their values. One central result, the line theorem, fixes the policy at every state except one. As the remaining state's policy varies, the resulting value functions trace a line segment. This connects a restricted change in decision behavior to a simple shape in value-function space.

The authors use this geometric perspective to introduce visualizations of reinforcement learning dynamics. These visualizations aim to make the behavior of learning algorithms easier to understand by showing their relationship to the attainable value space. The contribution centers on the structure of that space and its explanatory uses, with the finite state-action setting defining the scope of the stated results.
icml-2019-the-value-function-polytope-in.tldr: The attainable value functions of a finite Markov decision process form a general polytope, enabling geometric explanations of reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A classifier may satisfy a fairness requirement or a target false-positive rate on its training data yet fail to satisfy it at evaluation time. This paper studies that constraint-generalization problem. The setting covers data-dependent requirements used for fairness, reducing churn, and other policy goals alongside ordinary predictive training.

The proposed approach formulates constrained learning as a two-player game. One player updates model parameters using a training dataset, while the other enforces constraints using an independent validation dataset. Separating these responsibilities across datasets gives constraint enforcement its own evidence, rather than relying entirely on the data used for model optimization.

Building on two-player constrained optimization, the authors show that this two-dataset design can significantly improve how constraints generalize. Experiments illustrate that the benefit also appears in practice. The result concerns improved satisfaction of constraints on evaluation data; it does not turn training-time compliance into an unconditional guarantee. The independence of the validation dataset is a stated part of the proposed approach.
icml-2019-training-well-generalizing-cla.tldr: A two-player method separates model training from constraint enforcement on independent data to improve evaluation-time fairness and other constraint satisfaction.
